Abstract
              
                Background
                One of the main challenges for the CRISPR-Cas9 system is selecting optimal single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs). Recently, deep learning has enhanced sgRNA prediction in eukaryotes. However, the prokaryotic chromatin structure is different from eukaryotes, so models trained on eukaryotes may not apply to prokaryotes.
              
              
                Results
                We designed and implemented a convolutional neural network to predict sgRNA activity in Escherichia coli. The network was trained and tested on the recently-released sgRNA activity dataset. Our convolutional neural network achieved excellent performance, yielding average Spearman correlation coefficients of 0.5817, 0.7105, and 0.3602, respectively for Cas9, eSpCas9 and Cas9 with a recA coding region deletion. We confirmed that the sgRNA prediction models trained on prokaryotes do not apply to eukaryotes and vice versa. We adopted perturbation-based approaches to analyze distinct biological patterns between prokaryotic and eukaryotic editing. Then, we improved the predictive performance of the prokaryotic Cas9 system by transfer learning. Finally, we determined that potential off-target scores accumulated on a genome-wide scale affect on-target activity, which could slightly improve on-target predictive performance.
              
              
                Conclusions
                We developed convolutional neural networks to predict sgRNA activity for wild type and mutant Cas9 in prokaryotes. Our results show that the prediction accuracy of our method is improved over state-of-the-art models.

Abstract

Background
A key challenge in the CRISPR-Cas9 system is choosing optimal single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs). Deep learning has recently improved sgRNA prediction in eukaryotes. However, because prokaryotic chromatin structure differs from that of eukaryotes, models trained on eukaryotes may not transfer to prokaryotes.

Results
We developed and implemented a convolutional neural network to predict sgRNA activity in Escherichia coli. The network was trained and evaluated on a newly released sgRNA activity dataset. Our convolutional neural network performed excellently, with average Spearman correlation coefficients of 0.5817, 0.7105, and 0.3602 for Cas9, eSpCas9, and Cas9 with a recA coding region deletion, respectively. We verified that sgRNA prediction models trained on prokaryotes do not apply to eukaryotes, and vice versa. Perturbation-based methods were used to examine distinct biological patterns between prokaryotic and eukaryotic editing. We then improved predictive performance for the prokaryotic Cas9 system through transfer learning. Finally, we found that potential off-target scores accumulated across the genome affect on-target activity, which could modestly improve on-target predictive performance.

Conclusions
We developed convolutional neural networks for predicting sgRNA activity in prokaryotes, covering wild-type and mutant Cas9. Our findings show that this method achieves better prediction accuracy than state-of-the-art models.
